text: In the 1880s an income of £250 to £500 a year was enough for a respectable, even comfortable, middle-class household.
exceptions: Debts, a mortgage, or the cost of keeping up a large old house could swallow such an income.

text: Someone who takes a tooth-brush on a journey expects to sleep away from home.
exceptions: It may be a precaution in case of delay, or said in jest.

text: In a country district, hired drivers and inn people talk about the strangers they carry.
exceptions: Some are discreet or can be paid to keep quiet.

reads: It was nearly one o’clock when Sherlock Holmes returned from his excursion
text: Holmes is back at nearly one, carrying notes and figures from his errand.

reads: I have seen the will of the deceased wife
text: The Doctors' Commons guess was right. His errand was to read the mother's will.

reads: The total income, which at the time of the wife’s death was little short of £ 1,100, is now, through the fall in agricultural prices, not more than £ 750.
text: The income was nearly £1,100 when the mother died and is now at most £750.

reads: Each daughter can claim an income of £ 250, in case of marriage.
text: Each daughter can claim £250 a year on marriage.
£750 less £250 leaves £500 if one daughter marries, and £250 if both do. With Julia dead and unmarried, only one claim remains, so Helen's wedding would cost him a third of his present income.

reads: he has the very strongest motives for standing in the way of anything of the sort
text: The figures I wanted are in, and they back the money motive. Each marriage takes a large slice of his income, which makes his calm about both engagements harder to take at face value.

reads: this beauty would have had a mere pittance
text: 'Pittance' and 'cripple' are Holmes's words. £500, or even £250, was a decent income for many households. The motive looks strongest once the mortgaged house and his habits are counted, and we have no figures for those.

reads: it has proved that he has the very strongest motives
text: What is proved is the motive and nothing more. The will shows why he might want the marriages stopped. It does not show that he stopped Julia's, or how anyone could reach her in a sealed room.

Who gained from Julia's death? As Holmes reports the will, each daughter has her own £250, payable on marriage, and nothing suggests Julia's share passed to Helen. On these figures Roylott is the one who kept the money.

Helen said he has the money 'while we resided with him'. Holmes does not say what happens if a daughter dies or simply moves out. If leaving the house costs him too, that may be why their visits away needed his leave.

reads: I should be very much obliged if you would slip your revolver into your pocket.
text: Holmes has Watson take his revolver to Stoke Moran.

reads: this is too serious for dawdling, especially as the old man is aware that we are interesting ourselves in his affairs
text: Holmes laughed at the poker, but now he wants a gun along and is in a hurry. Having seen the figures and been visited by Roylott, he expects him to act and perhaps to turn violent.

reads: That and a tooth-brush are, I think, all that we need.
text: The arrangement with Helen was only to see over the rooms in the afternoon, yet a tooth-brush means a night away. Holmes may already intend to stay near the house overnight, possibly in the house itself.

reads: drove for four or five miles through the lovely Surrey lanes
text: Four or five miles from Leatherhead fits Helen's times for the drive this morning.

Four or five miles from Leatherhead is nowhere near the western border of Surrey. The drive and the times agree with each other, so the 'western border' is the loose part of her description. Nothing in the case seems to hang on it.

reads: It was a perfect day
text: The spring weather is there for contrast with the errand.

reads: There is some building going on there
text: This looks like the first outside sign that the repairs are real, though Watson describes only gables and a roof among the trees. Even if work is going on, that does not say it was needed.

reads: the trap rattled back on its way to Leatherhead
text: They send the trap away and arrange no return. That is a small point in favour of their staying the night.

reads: that this fellow should think we had come here as architects, or on some definite business
text: Roylott has already traced Helen once, and local drivers are the sort of people who could tell him things. Holmes is covering the reason for the visit.
So the remark about building was said for the driver's benefit. It gives no independent evidence about the repairs, which still have to be looked at close to.

reads: Dr. Roylott has gone to town, and it is unlikely that he will be back before evening
text: Helen expects Roylott to stay away until evening.

reads: All has turned out splendidly.
text: She is cheerful because she does not yet know he traced her. She has come to no harm so far only because he is away, and the danger Holmes feared begins when he gets home.

reads: he has followed me, then
text: This is her conclusion, not something she saw. Roylott said only that he 'traced' her, and he had planned to come to town anyway. How he found Baker Street is still open.

reads: He is so cunning that I never know when I am safe from him
text: This is new. She first described him as 'absolutely uncontrollable', and now she, who lives with him, calls him cunning. That answers my doubt about whether the bellowing man could also be a patient planner, though it is still only her opinion.

reads: he may find that there is someone more cunning than himself upon his track
text: Holmes accepts 'cunning' and speaks of Roylott as his quarry. There is no more talk of gipsies.

reads: You must lock yourself up from him to-night.
text: Holmes tells Helen to lock herself in tonight.

A locked door did not save Julia. Her key was turned (¶44), the door was found fastened on the inside (¶56), and Helen is now in that same room. The advice guards against Roylott's fists, not against whatever killed her sister.

reads: If he is violent, we shall take you away to your aunt’s at Harrow.
text: Holmes said there was not a moment to lose and the whistle has begun again. Why does he make removing her conditional on violence, instead of taking her to Harrow at once?
options: He wants to see the rooms before deciding
He needs her to stay in place for some purpose of his own
He thinks open violence is the nearest danger

text: 'We shall take you away' is said about tonight, so Holmes means to be within reach after Roylott comes home. That fits the tooth-brush.

Open: what killed Julia in a sealed room, what the 'speckled band' was, what makes the whistle and the clang, why Julia's room matters, how cigar smoke got into it, whether the repairs were needed, how Roylott traced Helen, what his business in town is, and what Holmes intends for tonight.

Working picture: Roylott has a solid money motive and more cunning than his bluster suggests. He probably killed Julia to save her £250 a year, and he may have manoeuvred Helen into the same room to save hers. The danger comes to a head tonight, when he is home and Holmes is probably close by. The method is still blank, and the rooms are the next evidence.
options: Roylott kills by a quiet means that reaches into the room without anyone entering
Roylott uses a drug or poison the doctors failed to detect
Roylott has the motive but Julia's death had another cause
